posts.content_md:
No, the number of excited atoms of course depends on pumping. Increasing pumping increases the population inversion and with this the small-signal gain g0 which is the gain the amplifier has for very small input powers. 

But the real gain you see is heavily dependent on input laser intensity because the amplification process itself lowers the population inversion and therefore decreasing gain. The saturation intensity is

 Isat=(h*f)/(t*d) (sorry cant write greek letters here) 

with h : planck constant 

f: frequency

t: upper laser level lifetime 

d: stimulated emission cross section, i. e. the "size" the atom has that a photon can hit and stimulate another photon. the last two are material constants.

The real gain coefficient is g = g0/(1+(I/Isat)) ( I : intensity of the input laser beam)

Yes that means the wings of a gaussian are amplified more than the center, but the effect of saturation is independent of pumping which only affects g0.

But you probably wont get a flat top through this if the input beam is gaussian. The output beam might be a more or less distorted gaussian but still very gaussian looking like.

Dear Holographers,

I have run some very high power tests on the SSY-1 pulsed laser.

Setup ----

SSY-1 modifications: Brewster window added and Cr4+:YAG passive q-switch replacing q-switch dye cell. Both done internal to the cavity.

PFN is totally replaced with a much higher uF and custom inductor.

There is no beam spreader optic right now, and the Joule meter measures the green power pulse just after the IR blocking lens which is Reflection coated for 1064nm. It is not coated for AR in 532nm though so a good amount is lost.

Here are some results of the tests tonight:

<500V no firing of the lamp

500V gives 40mJ of green

550V gives 84mJ

600V gives 123mJ

650V gives 127mJ

700V gives 160mJ

750V gives 175mJ

**800V gives 214mJ of green**

I was firing about once every 5 - 15 seconds, and about 3-7 times for each setting. The flashlamp snapped safely in the chamber at my 6th firing at 800 Volts. No doubt I require more time for the passively air cooled cavity to release the built-up temperature.

At 700V, I was injecting 30.63 Joules to the lamp, at 20.04% explosion energy (estimate).

At 800V, I was injecting 40 Joules to the lamp, at 26.16% explosion energy (estimate).

It does not seem that anything else was damaged except the lamp. Later I will replace it, and see how many times it fires at higher voltages (900 max), but allowing much longer to cool. The metal cavity housing was only a little warm to the touch. 

So I bet that the maximum for this setup will be about 1/4 Joule of 532 nm green output, polarized, and over 4-20ns (unmeasured as yet). Lifetime tests will need to be rigged up to run automatically.

There are better lamps available as well that might be used as a replacement in the future.

So to recap, the SSY-1, with $140 of enhanced parts, and a custom PFN $50, should be able to output 0.25 Joules of green. It is not certain for how long it needs to cool between shots. Also not sure of the quality of holograms this would make. 

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen

posts.content_md:
Transversal modes are beam profile patterns. in the fundamental TEM00 mode the beam has a gaussian shape and best divergence and smallest focus size. Higher order modes have patterns with more than one spot. Real laser beams can be a mixture of several modes. An aperture in the resonator can block higher order modes because they have a larger radius, thats what a cr:yag *might* do when it bleaches only in the middle where the highest intensity is.

Usually its said you need TEM00 for holography. I personally dont know any reason for this right now, it might be that most lasers that arent even TEM00 wont work for other reasons for holography.

Longitudinal modes are frequencies in the laser beam. Only waves that are resonant, i. e. that build up a standing wave, in your resonator are amplified. The spacing between these modes can be calculated 

deltaf=c/2l ;c lightspeed; l resonator length

To have a long coherence length you need a single frequency. Many longitudinal modes would mean short coherence. 1 Mode wildly changing its frequency or several modes starting and ending lasing while your q-switch is open might be bad too.

Because of this its so interesting if your laser is forgiving enough so it still has a sufficient coherence length without an etalon selecting just 1 single longitudinal mode.

Your observation that you can get bright sparkles from reflections indicates that your film and chemistry is likely OK when fed the correct proportions of object and reference light. You might also try making a single beam grating using a mirror to bounce reference light at an angle into the film. This pretty much tells you what maximum brightness would look like.

Insufficient object light (relative to the reference) will definitely cause dim holos. To compensate, you can:

1) add more light to the object with mirrors or whatever

2) use a brighter object 

3) dim the reference beam (not always easy for single beam and for objects close to the plate)

4) Do an H1-H2 transfer - you have total ratio control here

5) Use a material more forgiving of poor ratios such as BB-plates or Ultimate. I've only used these for reflection holos, no idea how they work for transmission. For green, the new Fuji film looks promising.

The JD-2 developer, which really is the CWC2 developer, like almost all others, just doesn't work in the realm of high intensity, short duration exposures.

Yes Ed I used to see that high Intensity problem with pulsed Ruby and thought it was a fact of life you had to put up with. So when I started working with a ~300mj pulsed FD YAG about 12 years ago I was expecting to see it all again. But after 12 years using a 6nsec. 532nm pulse

it has not been noticeable with silver halide although I have not been making proper comparisons with CW lasers. So perhaps alot of the problem was to do with 694nm 

 Interestingly in a paper I am doing for the July symposium in wales I show a pulsed portrait of my dirty fingers holding a coin that was shot in undyed DCG with 1 pulse! Although 5pulses over half a second is much brighter. There is a hint that the incredibly small absorption of dichromate at 532nm may be particularly effective when delivered in a 6ns pulse! A case of HIE ---High Intensity Enhancement?

**for Bill**:Herewith is the dev formula I find fine for pulsed 532nm

That is a good article for interest. But I contend that the best way of dealing with ascorbate developer stock and it is a way we have been successfully using for some years in our labs is to "A and B" it. 

For A we have a 500ml bottle with: 

20g ascorbic acid 

3g Metol (4-methylaminophenol sulfate) 

and top it up with 500ml deionized water 

for B we have a 500 ml bottle of 

50g sodium carbonate anhydrous 

15g sodium hydroxide 

top up with 500 ml deionized water. 

(This one should be labeled "very caustic" ) 

Just use equal volumes of A and B from then on. 

Now there are 3 bonus points for using Metol instead of phenidone. 

1) is that phenidone is quite a strong silver halide solvent and tests have proved that metol gives brighter holograms. 

2)The second point is that metol has a hardening action on gelatin and its effect on speeding up the development time over what you would have with just alkaline ascorbate means that even notoriously soft emulsions 

juch as PFG-03 can be in and out of the developer bath into a stop bath (~5% acetic acid ) in around 20 seconds, before the gelatin is seriously attacked. Assuming of course your exposure level was good enough. 

3) Metol is a weaker reducing agent or developer than alkaline ascorbic acid. 

When Metol gets oxidized it goes really dark brown so this is a useful indicator to tell you when your bath is exhausted because it wont go severely dark until most of the ascorbate has been oxidized. A mild yellowing like weak tea is quite OK . Only when the stuff gets to the colour of strong British tea without milk do you chuck it out. ) 

Dont forget to use the floating dish method of 2 closely fitting plastic dishes with the upper dish keeping most of the air out as it floats and acting as convenient agitator as well. 

Acid ascorbate in the stock soln A will not seriously oxidize for a long time 

(Slight yellowing is perfectly OK and can be ignored., provided your stuff does contain Metol.)

Dear Holographers,

If you place the spatial lens after the KTP and IR blocking mirror, then you don't get sparking with either the standard PFN (15 Joules to lamp) or my modified PFN (50 Joules to lamp).

If you place a lens before or without the KTP or IR blocking mirror, you run the risk of air sparking at the elevated powers. This arc looks white with a hint of blue, about 3 mm long and .7 mm wide. There is a considerable snapping noise when it arcs the air. This focal point is where you can burn through a razor blade (gillette). This would definitely ruin a pinhole, or create one in a piece of metal. That might be handy.

There is a possibility that I might be severely overexposing my films. I have noted that the exposed film will darken to 50% in a range of 15 to 90 seconds. I have been using JD-2 developer. This might be a bit fast fo0r this less sensitive developer, denoting an overexposed film. 

I will have to try some "underexposures" with the new developers. Also I need to try out a bigger KTP crystal since mine is 1mm diameter too small, and I get reflection artifacts and lines as the beam exits the KTP. The spatial filter does not clear them up!

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen

Dear Holographers,

There was actually nothing wrong with my modified SSY-1 with brewster, adjustable Etalon, and Cr4+:YAG passive q-switch. I was running it with the weaker PFN1 pulse forming network, and forgot that the lasing threshold of that system was higher because of the Cr4+:YAG q-switch. More energy is needed to open the switch, so 900 Volts gave 20mJ.

I have begun to eliminate optical components in the modified system to see if I can get comparably good holograms without them. I took a new SSY-1 unit and only put in the brewster window (to polarize the beam, and make KTP conversion of IR to green more efficient, a must).

Testing the unit now, I found that the original passive dye cell q-switch that is standard in the SSY-1, has a lower lasing threshold, and verified that it would lase down to 550 volts. At 900 volts I saw the same 20 mJ of green output I had with the modified system once I tweaked with the KTP alignment and Spatial Filter alignment. I have opted to repeat making holograms at this same exposure and other parameters.

My first tests failed because of my Metol solution was depleted, but showed that shorter time in the developer does not help. When I took a hologram at half the Metol development time of 90 seconds, there was an image, but dim. At 3 minutes of Metol only a little bit brighter. I figured out that the Metol was depleted to I changed the Metol solution to try again.

I had success with the next two. I took the hologram at 1 minute of Metol developer of my eyelid, forehead, eyebrows, nose, without glasses but eyes closed. Amazingly the detail was all there, and even more than my modified system. Still a splotchy and dirty image as usual, I'll discuss that below. I could make out all the individual hairs on my eyebrow closest to the film. I could not get a good picture of it to show you.

The second good one is pictured below. It is still 20mJ exposure, with 1 minute in Metol developer. My fingers hold a shiny quarter. You can read all of the quarter and see the shape of the head and details nice if you peer around in the unsplotchy areas. It is hard to take a picture that shows all the details at once.

**I believe that this shows that the pulsed holography system based on the SSY-1 needs only the brewster window to be added ($70) to work good. Also the cheap standard PFN1 can be used, and not the high power custom one I designed. This drastically reduces the cost and labor to modify it for holography.**

Next I will attempt to improve the image quality. Up till now, that has not been my emphasis. I mainly wanted to prove that this cheap system could produce green beams that were strong enough and fast enough to capture a living subject. I believe that this has been confirmed. The cause of the poor image quality may be sixfold. 

First, the KTP is only 4mm x 4mm and the laser beam is 5mm diameter. I noticed that this clipped and distorted the output green beam with interference lines that show up in all the holograms so far. (as a side note, I think I have designed a multi-axis KTP holder that is adjustable very simply and really cheap to make.)

Secondly, my beam expanding beam lens has always been damaged: it has a fracture in the center interior of the material (CaF2) which creates a blank starlike blotchy areas on all the holograms, so that the image disappears in this location. 

Thirdly, the green beam spreading lens is dirty. 

Fourth, the playback green laser dpss and lens I use to display and photograph the holograms is very poor with dirt all over it. 

Fifth, my spatial filter is out of alignment.

Sixth, I may need to add an aperture inside the SSY-1 cavity to select a fewer number of resonant frequencies of IR. I could use advice on this point.

These modifications will take some time and money, so they will have to wait till I can raise some money to buy the parts I need. Anyone know where I can get 5mm x 5mm KTP for pretty cheap? Will Edmunds Scientific glass lenses work for green beam spreading? Am I forgetting something?

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen

OK, now I have a new problem....

Examining the 50 micron aperture of my spatial filter, I noticed that all my testing had blown the hole very wide. In effect, the spatial filter in this state was doing nothing for ANY of my holograms so far.

Thinking that I ruined it by really pumping out the power with my previous hi energy PFN, and not blocking the IR that was not converted by the KTP crystal, I replaced the aperture.

The next aperture I put in was a smaller 25 micron one. I was bringing my lens towards the aperture and was noticing for the first time that the green projected spot was actually looking even and gaussian!

Hi Holographers,

I am doing calculations on an internal aperture (a drilled hole in a piece of sheet metal) inside the SSY-1 cavity that would force the TEM00 mode.

Colin alerted me to p.208 of Solid State Laser Engineering by W. Koechner formula for the Fresnel Number calculation. This number allows you to determine which sized internal aperture will force the TEM00 operation of a particular Nd:YAG rod geometry.

Fresnel numbers of less than 1 or even 2 will make TEM00 predominate, which is necessary for good holography.

N (=fresnel number) = (aperture radius^2)/(wavelength x rod length)

For the standard SSY-1 with no aperture we have N = ((2.5 mm ^2)*((1,000,000 nm/mm))/(1064 nm) *(60 mm)) = 98 which is quite poor.

If we add a 0.7 mm hole we get an N=2 which is good!

If we do not add an aperture but move one of the mirrors away, we can get an N=2 with a OC to HR distance of about 3 meters which seems impractical.

Remember that there might be a small aperture effect from having a passive q-switch in place. The intensity before lasing is strongest in the center which acts like an aperture. This makes TEM00 predominate. Then as the aperture opens, the rest of the excited rod acts like a self-amplifying rod to reinforce the TEM00 mode. But this is just conjecture. In any case, I am getting holograms (even though they are dim or maybe not fully TEM00) without an aperture.

If I follow Colin's advice of a 1 mm aperture in the cavity, my 30mJ energy would be reduced to about 1.5 mJ which is probably not enough to expose the plate (although the TEM00 energy would probably increase the quality of the dim holograms, a test is in order). If I use my enhanced PFN, then 150 mJ gets reduced to 7.5 mJ of TEM00 which I predict would give very good holograms. If the passive q-switch is helping the aperture and fresnel problem, maybe bigger apertures can be used and still have nearly TEM00 mode predominate (more experiments are needed) while using the cheaper and standard PFN1.

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen

The spatial filter tungsten aperture may come in today, and I will see if it cleans up the green beam that will be used for making holograms.

I have been reading "Solid-State Laser Engineering" by W. Koechner and found the following things:

**The presence of a passive q-switch favors single longitudinal mode of TEM00.** (reference p.511) This apparently applies to both dye cells and Cr4+:YAG.

Page 253-4 states that it was learned early on that the passive (dye) q-switches tend to act as TEM00 mode selectors. It was described by W. R. Sooy in Applied Physical Letters Volume 7, p.36 (1965). (Anyone able to get this article?) There are two things that both help in the generation of the TEM00 mode in the SSY-1:

1) Longitudinal mode selection in the laser takes place while the pulse is building up from noise. During this time, modes which have a higher gain or lower loss will increase in amplitude more rapidly than the unwanted modes. The higher gain waves (TEM00) bleach out the dye faster and as the aperture in the q-switch opens, it reinforces the TEM00 mode.

2) The greater the number of round trips that any particular mode takes in the laser cavity, the more it is reinforced. Since the q-switch allows multiple passes while it is opening, you get great reinforcement of the single most powerful mode. It is superior to a Pockels cell q-switch in mode selection for the reason that that cell opens rapidly all at once and does not let the waves have many passes in the cavity.

There was an example on page 511 of an Nd:YAG laser for space-borne high-resolution Lidar that exhibited this TEM00 mode selection. It was a diode pumped, 13mm long Nd:YAG laser with brewster angles on the rod (slab actually). There was a Cr4+:YAG passive q-switch (with 32% initial transmittance and 72% open bleached transmittance) in the cavity just behind the output coupler mirror. **That laser produced a TEM00 beam**with an output energy of 0.85 mJ over 1.4ns up to 100 Hz.

*Because of these findings, I am opting not to add an internal aperture to the SSY-1 laser cavity for now. I need as much energy as I can get.*

I have not seen it in print, but I think there is another factor involved in favoring TEM00 mode with a passive q-switch. The central (or a spot slightly skewed towards the flashlamp side in the SSY-1) area of the q-switch begins to bleach out first, acting as a small Fresnel number aperture. Then, that TEM00 energy builds up rapidly from the center outwards. More and more cross sectional area of the rod begins to sympathetically dump its energy into the TEM00 mode. This is possibly similar to having a second laser amplifier rod, which some of our esteemed collegues have suggested.

Any thoughts?

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen

Dear Holographers,

I have read the above pdf article called: The Natural Selection of Modes in a Passive Q-Switched Laser. Here are my conclusions:

We are comparing 2 techniques for generating ns pulses which can be used for green pulse holography. 

The first method, which is proven inferior, is Active Q-switching examples: acoustooptic modulator, pockels cells, or rotating mechanical mirror q-switch, or our common sense beliefs on laser operations). 

The second method is Passive Q-switching using bleachable dyes (as in the standard SSY-1) or as otherwise shown, the Cr4+:YAG passive q-switch.

The analysis and math are based on the numbers of transits that occur by the growing wave modes just before the lasing occurs. As you recall, the mode selection of TEM00 has been shown to depend favorable to these number of transits, but also the higher gain associated with the TEM00 mode energy (which is not considered in this paper).

The number of transists just before lasing is 21 times more selective for TEM00 mode in passive q-switches than with active q-switching. After subsequent lasing occurs, the difference grows non-linearly to over **2100 times more favoring of the TEM00 mode using passive q-switching than with active q-switching.**

This factor is further increased by an unknown amount if we consider the higher Gain inherent with the TEM00 wave over higher order modes.

**Conclusion: Probably don't need an internal aperture to force the TEM00 mode in a standard SSY-1 laser, used for holography.** It is possible that it might be running in nearly TEM00 mode already! That may be why we can make holograms with it in the first place.

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen
